questions.question: Describe the monopolist's equilibrium in words, explaining why marginal revenue lies below average revenue and how price, output and long-run profit compare with perfect competition.
questions.expected_answer: The monopolist is the industry, so it faces the downward-sloping market demand curve (D = AR) and is a price maker. Because selling one more unit requires lowering the single price on all units, marginal revenue is the new unit's price minus the revenue sacrificed on all previous units — e.g. moving from 10 units at R20 to 11 at R19 raises revenue from R200 to R209, so MR is R9 against a R19 price. The MR curve therefore falls below and twice as steeply as demand. Equilibrium follows the universal rule: produce where MR equals MC; the price is then read off the demand curve directly above that quantity, and profit is judged by comparing price with average cost there. Compared with perfect competition: price is above marginal cost, output is smaller than the competitive level, and because entry is blocked by legal barriers, resource ownership, natural monopoly or scale, economic profit can persist into the long run — the basis of the welfare complaint that consumers pay more for less.

questions.question: Explain the kinked demand curve of oligopoly, the resulting price stickiness and non-price competition, and distinguish overt from tacit collusion with South African examples.
questions.expected_answer: Oligopolists are few and mutually interdependent, so each firm's demand curve kinks at the ruling price. Above the kink demand is elastic: if one firm raises its price, rivals do not follow and its customers desert. Below the kink demand is inelastic: if it cuts price, rivals must match, so volumes barely change while everyone's revenue falls. Raising loses alone and cutting gains nothing, so prices are sticky — the kink even breaks the MR curve with a vertical gap, so modest cost changes leave price unchanged. Competition therefore migrates to non-price weapons: branding, advertising, loyalty programmes, features, service and sponsorships. Overt collusion is a cartel — an explicit agreement to fix prices or divide markets, acting jointly as a monopolist, as in South Africa's bread cartel and the World Cup construction bid-rigging, both punished under the Competition Act. Tacit collusion is wordless coordination such as price leadership, where a dominant firm moves and others follow. Cartels are inherently unstable because each member gains by secretly undercutting the agreed price.

questions.question: Explain the long-run equilibrium of monopolistic competition, including excess capacity, and compare the four market structures on entry and long-run profit.
questions.expected_answer: In monopolistic competition many sellers offer differentiated products, giving each a gently downward-sloping demand curve and short-run equilibrium like a small monopoly: output where MR = MC, price off the demand curve, with economic profit possible. But entry is free, so profit attracts imitators; each entrant slices away customers, shifting the incumbent's demand curve leftward until it is tangent to the average cost curve. At the tangency price equals average cost, so only normal profit remains. Because the demand curve slopes, the tangency lies on the falling part of AC, left of its minimum: firms carry excess capacity, producing less than the cost-minimising output — and price still exceeds marginal cost, so both efficiencies fail mildly, compensated by variety for consumers. Comparison: entry is free in perfect and monopolistic competition, difficult in oligopoly and blocked in monopoly; consequently long-run economic profit is impossible in the first two (competed away by entry) but possible in oligopoly and persistent in monopoly. Control over price runs from none (price taker) through slight and considerable to full price maker, and the firm's demand curve from horizontal through gently sloping and kinked to the market demand curve itself.
